description:
We are a team of like-minded people who are interested in space and everything related to it, and we also love board games :)

The team will include Dad, Mom, me (11 years old), school friends, and an acquaintance who in his youth  wanted to work in space, wrote to NASA (in the 90s, Uzbekistan) but was unsuccessful, and still is interested in space. I live in Russia.
summary:
Space Mission Design Game turns mission design into a playable fifteen-step campaign. You take an objective - a target point, a science goal, a deadline and a treasury — and have to return a spacecraft that can be built, launched and operated: launcher, attitude control, power, thermal, onboard recorder, instruments, antennas, ground stations. Every card immediately recalculates the whole chain: mass against  the launcher's payload, power against the operating mode, data against the downlink, money against the deadline. The output is not a grade but a probability: success chance, science, points, rating at risk.
A mission is not a single dice roll - after acceptance it flies for one to four steps, each a communication session with incidents, data recovery and science. Four roles (manager, engineer, scientist, flight controller) split the decisions, so a team has to negotiate. The same rulebook exists as a printable tabletop edition - 90 cards, an A3 board, tokens - for classrooms without computers.
Balance is calibrated by Monte Carlo: 150 games × 10 missions, average rating 81.4, failure share 32.6%.
details:
What the project does

The game puts a student in the seat of a mission designer and keeps them there for fifteen steps.

An objective is a target point (low Earth orbit, geostationary, the Moon, Mars, the asteroid belt, deep space), a science goal, a deadline and a treasury. The answer has to be a spacecraft that can actually be built, launched and operated: launcher, attitude control, structure and modules, redundant units, power sources, thermal control, onboard recorder, instruments, antennas, buffer and ground facilities.

A build is described by six numbers that fight over the same margin - launch mass, power, data volume, downlink, money and time - plus a failure probability and a deterministic science value.

There is no "correct" build. The reference builds for the same objective range from a cheap low-risk design with a poor science return to an ambitious one that is one subsystem away from failure, and both are legitimate answers to the same contract.

One engine, `data/engine.js`, is a set of pure functions with no dependencies. Every screen - browser, command-line validator, Monte Carlo - calls the same functions, so a rule can never mean two different things in two places.


How it works

Role HQ
(`app/index.html`) - four roles with separate signatures (manager, engineer, scientist, flight controller), SVG build graphs, a consultant that lists blockers and risks, chat and notes.

Calculator
(`calc/index.html`) - mission > trajectory > build > checks > success probability, science, rating delta. This is the teaching screen: every number is visible and explained by a tooltip.

Campaign v1.5
(`calc/campaign.html`) - fifteen steps (12 or 18 optional) over MCC levels, the factory, the school, R&D and competence levels, tests and stand runs, ground contracts, flights and acceptance, then the final score.

Team room
(`server/` + `app/lobby.html` + `app/play.html`) - up to four players, live updates over server-sent events, archive and leaderboard. Node 24, no dependencies, no keys.

Tabletop edition
(`print/`) - 90 cards at 63×88 mm, an A3 board, tokens and A4 sheets, generated
from the same data files, so paper and screen cannot drift apart.

The flight phase is the part that matters most.

Acceptance rolls the channel probability once; after that the
mission flies - two steps for the Moon, three for Mars and the belt, four for deep space - and each step is a communication session: channel load against MCC capacity, incidents, data recovery (75% floor from the onboard recorder), science. Flying longer is not a second chance at the dice; it costs time, and time is the treasury. Flight events are checked against the build rather than chosen by the player: the onboard recorder answers a solar flare, a duplicated attitude-control unit answers a micrometeorite, a trained school answers a software error.

Who benefits

Students and teachers
- a full mission-design loop that fits a lesson. The campaign length switches between 12, 15 and 18 steps; the calculator alone is a ten-minute exercise.

Clubs, museums, science circles
- the tabletop edition needs no computers, no accounts and no network: print, cut, play. One facilitator can run a room with the chat-GM tool.

Small teams that want a
design-review warm-up - the consultant and the checks work like a review: they name the blocker and the risk instead of giving a score.

Anyone who wants to look inside the model - the engine, the numbers and the balance
report are in the repository; `node tools/check.mjs 150` reproduces the calibration in a couple of minutes.

How NASA data is used

The 27 mission cards are real missions, and each one carries its launch year, agency, target point, data type, required equipment, historical outcome and a note explaining which rule the real outcome demonstrates. The full annotated list of sources is in §4. The design constraints - payload against target point, power per operating mode, data
volume against downlink, session windows against MCC capacity - follow the challenge brief and the public mission descriptions. No NASA imagery, logo or flag is redistributed; the art is original and generated locally.

Tools, languages and libraries

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript. No framework, no bundler, no runtime dependencies - the game runs from `file://` and from GitHub Pages.

Node 24 (ESM, built-in modules only) for the network server, the validators and the Monte Carlo.

Server-sent events for the live team room; SVG for the build graphs; `localStorage` plus JSON export/import for saves and for shareable campaign seeds.

ComfyUI with the Z-Image Turbo model and a Qwen3-4B text encoder for the illustrations; the prompts are in `art/prompts.json` (cards) and `demo/prompts.json` (deck backgrounds).

Git and GitHub Pages for versioning and hosting; the repository ships validators (`check`, `dom-check`, `lang-check`, `app-smoke`, `play-smoke`, `server-smoke`, `session selftest`) instead of a CI service.

What is creative about it

The card is the calculation.
There is no spreadsheet next to the game: playing a card recalculates mass, power, data, money, success probability, science, points and rating in one pass.

Failure is a property of the build,
not a dice throw. The interface shows which missing subsystem caused which incident, so a failed flight still teaches something.

A flight is a phase, not an instant.
One acceptance roll, then sessions that cost time and recover data — the trade-off moves from luck to scheduling.

Two editions from one source of
truth. The printed deck and the browser read the same data files, so a rule change cannot drift between paper and screen.

Public balance.
Targets, reference builds and the Monte Carlo are part of the repository: anyone can re-run the calibration and argue with the numbers.

History as a rules test.
Each real mission outcome is annotated with the rule it demonstrates Luna 3 lost frames are `D_ratio < 1`, Hubble's data stream needs a wide channel and a buffer.

Obstacles and what we changed

A design loop that fits fifteen
steps without becoming a spreadsheet. Every card states its effect on the resource chain; the arithmetic lives in the engine, the explanations live in tooltips.

Balance. Early
builds were either trivial or impossible. We set the targets first - average rating above 40, failure share 15-35%, launcher duplication below 40%, success probability 0.68-0.72 - and then tuned until the simulation sat in the corridor (now 81.4 / 32.6% / 30.1% / 0.687 over 150 games × 10 missions).

A flight that is not another dice
roll. This became the v1.5 redesign: one acceptance roll, sessions with channel load, a data-recovery floor, events checked against the build.

Paper and screen telling the same
story. The print sheets are generated from `data/cards.js`; the validators fail the build if a deck renders empty or shows `undefined`.

Limits.
The Monte Carlo does not model hiring, salaries or facility upgrades, and the
art pipeline needs a local ComfyUI - without it the cards print with blueprint placeholders. Both are stated in `README.md`.
